tldr: A framework where both a human and a dexterous robot hand wear the exact same exoskeleton mechanism, fundamentally eliminating kinematic and visual gaps and streamlining imitation learning for contact-rich dexterous manipulation.

overview:
In imitation learning for dexterous manipulation using multi-fingered hands, accurately transferring natural human demonstrations to the robot—the retargeting problem—has long been a major bottleneck. Camera-based hand tracking is vulnerable to occlusions and jitter during contact. Data gloves leave persistent errors due to skeletal differences. Moreover, existing exoskeleton approaches rely on unidirectional mapping models calibrated in free space, leading to large discrepancies between joint commands and actual motions when contact forces and friction occur. In addition, because humans and robots look different, complex processing using generative models has been required to inpaint or synthesize the hand appearance.

To tackle this, the authors arrived at an exceptionally straightforward idea: simply have both the human and the robot wear the exact same exoskeleton. They designed an exoskeleton that is isomorphic to the robot hand, sharing the same sensors, contact surfaces, and wrist camera placement across both human and robot. Consequently, differences between their encoder trajectories can be used directly as supervisory signals. Through paired replays of random motions in free space (motor babbling) and actual grasping motions, the system acquires a command mapping model that is robust to contact loads. Because the wrist cameras share the exact same egocentric perspective of the exoskeleton, policies can be trained directly on raw images without cumbersome image inpainting.

In real-robot experiments across five contact-rich, high-precision tasks—such as tightening screws with an electric screwdriver and inserting earbuds into an AirPods case—SEED-UMI achieved 3.0x greater data collection efficiency than exoskeleton-based teleoperation, with an average rollout success rate of 70.0%. Furthermore, on tasks requiring delicate positioning and precise timing, it proved capable of outperforming teleoperation plagued by communication latency.
contributions: Proposed the "Shared Physical Measurement" paradigm, where both the human and robot hand wear an identical exoskeleton.
Developed a hardware design using a four-bar linkage mechanism to preserve clearance on the palm and finger sides while achieving exact one-to-one joint correspondence and identical contact geometry.
Constructed an encoder-to-command mapping model that tracks accurately even under contact loads through two-stage training with motor babbling and paired replay under contact.

Demonstrated direct end-to-end policy learning from raw wrist images without image generation or segmentation, achieving 3x the data collection speed of teleoperation and an average success rate of 70.0%.

sections.heading: Breaking Through the Retargeting Wall in Dexterous Hand Learning
sections.summary: The biggest hurdle in imitation learning for multi-fingered hands lies in retargeting and demonstration collection across the human-robot embodiment gap. This paper introduces SEED-UMI, which turns retargeting into direct supervised learning by having both human and robot wear the same exoskeleton to share sensors and contact geometry.
sections.details:
In robot learning, control of wheeled bases and single arms has advanced rapidly, but dexterous manipulation with high-DOF multi-fingered hands remains a major challenge. The bottleneck lies in demonstration collection and retargeting—transferring natural human hand movements onto the robot. This is because humans and robots differ fundamentally in link lengths, joint axes, ranges of motion, and contact dynamics.

Conventional collection methods all have trade-offs. Vision-based hand tracking is natural to wear, but suffers from occlusions and jitter upon contacting objects. Data gloves provide stable joint measurements, but skin deformation causes substantial errors that require complex remapping. Exoskeleton devices allow accurate joint measurements, but tend to be bulky and restrict motion. Furthermore, existing exoskeleton approaches (such as DexUMI) rely on unidirectional mappings from human movements to the robot, calibrated in free space under no load. As a result, tracking severely breaks down once contact forces and friction come into play. They also depend on generative inpainting models to bridge the visual discrepancy.

To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes the "Shared Physical Measurement" approach. Instead of forcing software to bridge human-robot physical differences, both the human and the robot wear an exoskeleton that is isomorphic to the robot hand. This aligns all 20-DOF encoder measurements and wrist camera viewpoints entirely in hardware. Consequently, high-quality imitation learning is made possible using only raw wrist images and encoder signals, without any visual generative pipeline.

sections.heading: How It Differs from Prior Work: Exoskeletons, Visual Alignment, and Mapping
sections.summary: Prior exoskeletons were worn only on the human side, requiring generative models to resolve visual differences. SEED-UMI structurally removes visual gaps by putting the exoskeleton on the robot as well, learning contact-aware command mappings purely from real-world data without simulation or reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
Related work in this area broadly falls into three categories:

### Demonstration Collection via Wearable Exoskeletons
Data gloves can measure hand poses, but lack a one-to-one correspondence with robot joints. In contrast, robot-matched exoskeletons (such as DexUMI and WHED) enable high-precision measurement. However, these systems have the exoskeleton worn only by the human, relying on one-shot regression calibrated in free space to transfer to the robot. SEED-UMI places the identical exoskeleton on the robot hand too, converting the open-loop mapping problem into supervised learning using paired real-world data.

### Visual Alignment for Cross-Embodiment Learning
To bridge visual differences between human and robot hands, prior works often used inpainting techniques to generatively redraw the hand into a robot hand. In SEED-UMI, both human and robot wear the same exoskeleton, and wrist cameras are rigidly fixed to it. As a result, the externally visible mechanism, manipulated objects, and contact interfaces are virtually identical from the start. Policies can therefore be trained on raw images with standard data augmentations, without needing hand segmentation or image generation.

### Mapping from Encoders to Motor Commands
Free-space regression models easily fail under contact loads, while acquiring low-level controllers via simulation reinforcement learning (such as DexterityGen) always faces the sim-to-real gap. By replaying motions on the robot through the identical exoskeleton, SEED-UMI learns a contact-resilient mapping using direct real-world supervisory signals alone, bypassing both simulators and reinforcement learning.

captions.F2: The identical exoskeleton hardware worn by a human (left) and the fully actuated robot hand (right). Non-contact magnetic rotary encoders are placed at each joint. An Intel RealSense T265 for pose tracking on the dorsal side of the wrist and a fisheye camera for observing the hand on the palmar side are rigidly fixed in identical relative configurations.

sections.heading: Hardware Design: Putting the Same Mechanism on Human and Robot
sections.summary: A 20-DOF exoskeleton was designed to be kinematically isomorphic to the target robot hand. By utilizing a four-bar linkage to offset joint encoders to the dorsal side, the mechanism avoids obstructing lateral finger ranges of motion and palmar contact surfaces.
sections.details:
The SEED-UMI hardware is engineered so that when worn by either the human or the robot, external contact geometry and encoder coordinate frames match perfectly.

### 3.1 Exoskeleton Mechanism Design
Rather than aiming for a generic transfer tool, the exoskeleton was co-designed specifically for a single, fully actuated multi-fingered hand (the Wuji hand).

- ### Isomorphic Kinematic Skeleton (E.1)
Rotational joints correspond one-to-one with the active DOFs of the target hand, with link lengths and joint axis orientations strictly matched to the robot's phalanges. Mechanical hard stops are also aligned with the robot's range of motion, meaning the operator can move only within the exact envelope the robot can reach. Across all five fingers, a total of 20 independent joints are measured.
- ### Four-Bar Linkage for Encoder Placement (E.2)
Placing encoders directly beside joint axes causes the housings to protrude laterally, obstructing finger abduction/adduction and blocking palmar contact surfaces. To prevent this, the authors developed a four-bar linkage mechanism that transfers joint rotation to non-contact magnetic encoders located on the dorsal side of the hand (Figure F4 (b)). This leaves lateral and palmar contact areas completely open while preserving a true one-to-one rotational transmission between joint angles and encoder shafts.
- ### Shared Contact Geometry (E.3)
While attachment cuffs and mounts differ between human and robot setups, the outer skeletal frame, link lengths, and fingertip pad shapes are identical. Consequently, geometric interaction boundaries with objects match completely. Any discrepancy between human and robot encoder readings purely reflects load-dependent physical phenomena, such as contact forces, friction, and backlash.

### 3.2 Sensor Integration
All sensors are rigidly mounted to the exoskeleton frame.

- ### Joint Encoders (S.1)
Every joint is equipped with a non-contact magnetic encoder, producing a 20-dimensional vector $\mathbf{e}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{20}$. Because linkage tolerances introduce non-linearities between encoder readings and robot motor commands, these are corrected by the mapping model described in Section 4.
- ### Wrist Cameras (S.2)
An Intel RealSense T265 camera for 6-DOF tracking is placed on the dorsal side of the wrist, and a 150-degree FOV fisheye camera is mounted on the palmar side. Because they remain in the exact same relative position to the exoskeleton whether worn by a human or a robot, policy models can take raw images with clearly visible contact pixels directly as inputs without suffering from visual domain shift.

captions.F4: Exoskeleton mechanism design. (a) Before optimization (left), encoders beside the joints collided with each other (red); after optimization (right), ample clearance is maintained. (b) The four-bar linkage mechanism accurately transmits rotation angles to dorsal-mounted encoders without blocking palmar finger contact surfaces.

sections.heading: Two-Stage Mapping and Policy Learning to Bridge Contact Gaps
sections.summary: Converting exoskeleton encoder signals into robot motor commands is learned in two stages: free-space "motor babbling" and contact-rich "paired replay." Corrections from the resulting paired data eliminate tracking delays under contact loads, enabling the training of high-quality autonomous policies.
sections.details:
Even though identical encoder signals $\mathbf{e}_t$ are obtained on both human and robot, a mapping $\mathbf{e}_t \mapsto \mathbf{q}_t$ is required to convert them into actual robot joint motor commands $\mathbf{q}_t$. The proposed method learns this in two stages:

### M.1 Robot Motor Babbling
First, with the robot wearing the exoskeleton, it autonomously executes single-joint sweeps, coordinated movements, and self-contact poses in free space (motor babbling). By recording robot joint commands $\mathbf{q}_t$, robot-side encoder readings $\mathbf{e}_t^{(r)}$, and a history vector $\mathbf{h}_t$ (containing the past $K$ encoder steps, finite-difference velocities, and opening/closing direction flags), an initial mapping model $f_{\theta^0}: (\mathbf{e}_t, \mathbf{h}_t) \mapsto \mathbf{q}_t$ is fitted. However, because this is an unloaded free-space model, the fingers flex and deviate under load when contacting objects.

### M.2 Paired Replay and Fine-Tuning
Next, a human wears the exoskeleton to perform representative object grasps, collecting contact-rich encoder trajectories $\{\mathbf{e}_t^{(h)}, \mathbf{h}_t^{(h)}\}$. These motions are replayed on the robot using the initial model $f_{\theta^0}$, recording the resulting robot-side encoder values and commands as paired data. The discrepancies between the human's intended encoder trajectories and the robot's actual executed encoder trajectories serve as correction signals. Using a robot forward model $g_\phi$, the mapping model $f_\theta$ is fine-tuned to minimize an objective function comprising encoder matching, command regularization, and temporal smoothness. This allows the robot to reproduce the human's joint angles accurately even under contact loads.

### M.3 Policy Learning and Deployment
Autonomous control policies are trained using standard models such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, and $\pi_{0.5}$. Taking raw wrist camera images $I_t$ and encoder vectors $\mathbf{e}_t$ as inputs, the policy predicts chunks of 6-DOF wrist motions and 20-DOF hand joint commands. All training relies entirely on real human demonstration data, completely bypassing simulators and image inpainting.

### Qualitative Value of Direct Demonstrations
As shown in the AirPods insertion comparison in Figure F6, an operator in teleoperation cannot feel contact reaction forces, creating a risk of exerting excessive force on the robot side and damaging the object. In contrast, SEED-UMI captures direct demonstrations where the human operator benefits from immediate visual and tactile feedback, enabling delicate force regulation and recording highly precise contact motions.

captions.F3: Overview of the SEED-UMI pipeline. Demonstrations collected by a human wearing the exoskeleton are replayed on the robot using a free-space babbling model. The resulting internal/external encoder discrepancies are used to fine-tune the mapping model ($f_\theta$) before deploying to the final autonomous policy.
captions.F6: Comparison of replay encoder trajectories in the AirPods insertion task. Under SEED-UMI (left), human (blue) and robot (orange) trajectories match closely. Under conventional teleoperation (right), contact causes excessive pushing and overshoot (red dashed line).

sections.heading: Evaluated on Five Harsh Contact Tasks: 3x Speed, 70% Success Rate
sections.summary: Real-robot evaluations across five tasks—screw driving, AirPods insertion, ball throwing, table cleaning, and air freshener spraying—achieved 3x faster demonstration collection than teleoperation and an average success rate of 70.0%. Paired fine-tuning showed tremendous impact in correcting contact loads.
sections.details:
Real-world experiments were conducted using a RealMan RX75 arm paired with a 20-DOF Wuji hand to thoroughly evaluate the proposed approach.

### 5.1 Experimental Setup
The evaluation comprised five contact-rich, dexterity-demanding tasks (Figure F5):
- **Screw Driving**: Grasping an electric screwdriver, aligning it with a screw head, and maintaining downward pressure while driving the screw.
- **AirPods Case Insertion**: Coordinating index and middle fingers to pick up an AirPod and insert it precisely into a narrow slot in the charging case.
- **Ball Basket Throwing**: Grasping and lifting a ball from a table, then releasing it with precise timing to throw it into a target basket.
- **Table Cleaning**: Pulling out a tissue, wiping a table surface under sustained pressure, and disposing of it into a trash bin.
- **Air Freshener Spray**: Firmly supporting a spray can with multiple fingers while depressing the top actuator with the thumb.

Three conditions were compared: (1) real-time teleoperation using the exoskeleton (Teleoperation, T), (2) the proposed method without paired fine-tuning (P-), and (3) the full proposed pipeline (P+). For each task, 100 demonstration episodes were collected, and 20 autonomous rollouts were evaluated per condition and policy backbone.

### 5.2 Key Results and Analysis
- **Surpassing Teleoperation in Delicate and Dynamic Tasks (F1)**
Across all tasks and backbones, the average success rate of the proposed method (P+, 70.0%) was comparable to teleoperation (T, 71.7%). Remarkably, P+ outperformed teleoperation on tasks demanding fine positioning or high-speed timing, such as AirPods insertion (73.3% vs. 65.0%) and ball throwing (68.3% vs. 60.0%). While teleoperation suffers from communication latency and lack of haptic feedback that degrade precision, SEED-UMI lets humans manipulate objects directly with their hands, capturing superior demonstrations.
- **Paired Fine-Tuning Shines Under Contact Loads (F2)**
Moving from P- to P+ boosted average success from 57.3% to 70.0% (+12.7 points). Improvements were especially noticeable on tasks involving strong contact forces, including screw driving (+16.7 points), table cleaning (+15.0 points), and spraying (+15.0 points). This confirms that mapping trained purely in free space (P-) fails because it cannot compensate for finger deflection caused by contact loads.
- **3x Higher Collection Throughput (F3)**
In the AirPods task, SEED-UMI collected 52 successful demonstrations within 30 minutes, compared to just 18 for teleoperation—a 3.0x throughput gain. Because human operators work naturally without robot latency, data collection efficiency is vastly increased without sacrificing demonstration quality.

captions.F5: Rollout scenes from the five evaluated dexterous manipulation tasks on the real robot: stable screwdriver grasping, fine fingertip coordination for AirPods insertion, multi-finger handling of a spray can, precise throwing timing, and sustained-contact table cleaning.

sections.heading: A New Paradigm: Solving Embodiment Gaps with Shared Mechanisms
sections.summary: SEED-UMI demonstrates that sharing an identical exoskeleton between human and robot significantly accelerates imitation learning for contact-rich dexterous manipulation. Achieving 3x faster collection and a 70% success rate, it offers a compelling new paradigm for multi-fingered robot hand learning.
sections.details:
Rather than relying solely on software or complex generative vision models to bridge human-robot physical differences, this work demonstrates a fundamental alternative: sharing a common physical measurement interface.

Wearing the same exoskeleton guarantees kinematic correspondence and visual alignment at the hardware level. Paired replays in the real world then automatically produce mappings resilient to contact forces. Simultaneously outperforming teleoperation in collection throughput and delivering competitive success rates on demanding real-world contact tasks represents a significant milestone toward large-scale dexterous data collection.

sections.heading: Current Limitations: Hand Generalization and Wearability Challenges
sections.summary: The current design is tailored to a specific robot hand, requiring new hardware mechanisms for other models. Future challenges include improving donning/doffing ergonomics for long sessions and integrating tactile sensors for more direct contact estimation.
sections.details:
While the framework shows strong efficacy, several limitations remain:

- ### Lack of Generalization Across Robot Hands
The current exoskeleton is mechanically optimized specifically for the Wuji hand. Adapting to a different multi-fingered hand with different link lengths or joint topologies would require redesigning the exoskeleton and repeating the calibration procedure.
- ### Wearability and Ergonomic Hurdles
Because the human must physically wear the exoskeleton, the overhead of donning/doffing, the weight of the device, and operator fatigue during extended collection sessions may affect sustained or ultra-delicate tasks.
- ### Direct Sensing of Tactile Information
Contact compensation is currently inferred indirectly through load variations in joint encoders. Embedding tactile sensors into the fingertip pads could offer direct detection and compensation of contact forces and slippage.

takeaways: The retargeting problem can be dramatically simplified by sharing hardware (an isomorphic exoskeleton) rather than attempting to solve it purely in software.
Having the same mechanism on the outside of both human and robot removes visual domain gaps, allowing policies to learn directly from raw camera images.
Paired training using differences from contact replays—not just free-space motor babbling—is crucial for high success rates on contact tasks.
Allowing humans to demonstrate directly rather than through laggy teleoperation yields a ~3x data collection speedup and higher demonstration quality on delicate tasks.
limitations: The exoskeleton is tailored to a single specific robot hand, lacking mechanical generality across different hand models.
Because humans must wear the apparatus, donning/doffing overhead and operator physical fatigue remain non-negligible.
Tactile sensors are not integrated into the fingertips, leaving contact state estimation reliant on joint encoder behavior.
